name: The Gomero de la Recoleta

location.address: Av. Pres. Manuel Quintana 596, Plazoleta Juan XXIII, Recoleta

access: Free, standing in a public plazoleta a few metres from the Recoleta Cemetery gate, open at all hours
transport: About 10-15 minutes' walk from Subte Line D, Callao station; several bus lines (17, 60, 92, 130, 152) stop nearby
story:
One branch of this fig reaches thirty metres out from the trunk and is over a metre thick where it leaves it. Since 2014 a sculpture of Atlas, welded from car parts by the Uruguayan artist Joaquin Arbiza Brianza, has stood underneath it appearing to take the weight. The city government calls this the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, and nobody agrees on how it got here. One account has the Recoleto friars planting it around 1718. Another credits the agronomist Martin Jose de Altolaguirre, who kept an orchard of exotic species on this ground around 1781. Either version puts it here before Argentina was a country, a few metres from the gate of the Recoleta cemetery, watching two centuries of the city arrive to bury its dead.

The species is disputed as well. Porteños call it a gomero, a loose word attached to several big figs in Argentina. The city's own register describes Ficus macrophylla, the Moreton Bay fig, and its account of the leaves and fruit fits that; Wikidata files the same tree as Ficus elastica, the rubber tree. We have gone with the register and flagged the disagreement rather than settling it.

The measurements need reading carefully too. The seven metres quoted across its trunk is the buttressed, fused mass a strangler fig builds over time, not a single round stem, so the girth figure here is far larger than any ordinary waistline.
verify_notes_removed: OFFICIAL SOURCE: the city government's own Arbopedia register (buenosaires.gob.ar) lists this specific tree, at this address, with species Ficus macrophylla, height ~18m, trunk diameter 7m, branches up to 30m long and over 1m thick, leaves/flowers/fruit description matching macrophylla. Corroborated by El Destape (news), Billiken and BAE Negocios articles calling it the oldest tree in the City of Buenos Aires. SPECIES CONFLICT, flagged rather than resolved: Wikidata (Q56303696, 'Rubber Tree of Recoleta') and several tourist sources instead call it Ficus elastica (true rubber tree, a different species); 'gomero' is used as a loose common name for several large Ficus species in Argentina. Going with the city's own register description here since it is the most detailed botanical account and matches the buttressed, banyan-like growth habit of F. macrophylla, but the writer should note the discrepancy rather than assert species with full confidence. AGE: two competing planting stories, both about this specific specimen (not the surrounding garden): planted by the Padres Recoletos around 1718, or by agronomist engineer Martin Jose de Altolaguirre around 1781 when he kept an exotic-species orchard on the site. Age given as a broad band spanning both hypotheses. GIRTH: the register's '7m trunk diameter' is a buttressed/multi-stemmed mass typical of strangler figs, not a simple round trunk; converted to a circumference figure (7m x pi = ~22m = 2199cm) for girth_cm, but this is NOT a normal single-trunk girth and the writer should say so rather than quote it as a plain measurement. HISTORY: a car-parts sculpture of Atlas by Uruguayan artist Joaquin Arbiza Brianza, donated to the city in 2014, appears to hold up one of the tree's longest branches. The city page also notes similar, smaller gomeros in nearby Plaza San Martin de Tours believed to be descendants of this tree, a possible separate candidate worth checking. LOCATION: two independent coordinate readings (Wikidata vs. the famous-trees Commons sweep lead) sit about 45m apart inside the small Plazoleta Juan XXIII (bounded by Junin, Pte. Ortiz, Av. Quintana and Guido); no single satellite-confirmed pin, so marked approximate at the plaza's centre near the Quintana 596 address, honest rather than exact. Publicly visible for over two centuries and still alive per the government's own current listing and 2026 press coverage.

name: The Magnolias del Protomedicato

location.address: Humberto Primo 343, San Telmo (viewed from the street/church entrance opposite; the trees stand in the entrance garden of Escuela Guillermo Rawson)

access: View-only. Visible from Humberto Primo street and from the entrance of the Parroquia San Pedro Gonzalez Telmo church opposite (Humberto Primo 340); the two magnolias themselves stand inside the entrance garden of a working school, Escuela Dr. Guillermo Rawson, whose grounds are not open to the public
transport: Half a block from Plaza Dorrego, San Telmo; about 10 minutes' walk from Subte Line C, Independencia or San Juan stations
story:
These two magnolias are the oldest living thing on the block where Buenos Aires first taught medicine. They flank the entrance of a primary school built over the site of the Protomedicato, the Viceroyalty's medical tribunal founded by Miguel O'Gorman, which also held the city's first Hospital de Hombres and its first school of medicine. Argentina declared the pair Historic Trees by national decree in August 1969, and the city has looked after them since.

How old they are is an open argument, and the city's own register runs both ways on a single page. Its text says the Bethlemite order planted them at the end of the 19th century, which would make them around 140. The same page, and every other source that mentions them, says more than 200 years and ties them to the Bethlemites' 18th-century work on this ground. The likeliest reading is a slip between XVIII and XIX, so we carry the older claim with the doubt attached rather than picking a winner.

You look at these two rather than walk up to them. The school is in daily use and its grounds are closed to visitors, so the place to stand is Humberto Primo itself, or the doorway of the San Pedro Gonzalez Telmo church opposite, which is where the photographs get taken from. It is half a block from Plaza Dorrego, so the detour costs nothing.
verify_notes_removed: TWO TREES, ONE ENSEMBLE: a pair of Magnolia grandiflora flanking the entrance of a school (Escuela N.22 'Dr. Guillermo Rawson') built on the site of the Protomedicato, the Viceroyalty's medical tribunal founded by Miguel O'Gorman, and the first Hospital de Hombres and School of Medicine of Buenos Aires. Declared Arboles Historicos by National Decree No. 5241 of 12 August 1969, per the city's own Arbopedia register, Argentina.gob.ar and multiple press pieces (La Nacion, Infobae, Billiken). ACCESS, SCHOOL GROUNDS: this is a functioning primary school and its grounds are not open to the public. Treating this as VIEW-ONLY per the Hobart-oak precedent: the trees are genuinely visible from Humberto Primo street and, per the Infobae feature, tourists commonly photograph them 'desde la entrada de la iglesia' (from the church entrance opposite), so the pin marks that public viewing spot rather than the school garden itself. AGE DISCREPANCY, flagged rather than resolved: the city's own Arbopedia page text says the trees were 'plantadas a fines del siglo XIX' (planted late 19th century) by the Bethlemite order, which would make them only ~130-145 years old, yet the same page and every other source (Infobae, La Nacion, Argentina.gob.ar, Billiken) call them 'more than 200 years old' and tie them to the Bethlemite-run Protomedicato period, an 18th-century institution (founded ~1780, largely superseded after Argentine independence). A separate search result independently describes the site as 'occupied by the Bethlehemite order during the 18th century, with magnolia trees dating from that era still flanking its entrance,' which matches the repeated 200+ year claim and suggests the Arbopedia's own 'siglo XIX' is likely a typo for 'siglo XVIII'. Delivered with the repeated 'over 200 years' claim as the age_estimate (kept vague per source, not sharpened) and a broad age_min/age_max band; the writer should not present an exact planting decade with confidence. GIRTH: no trunk diameter or circumference given by any source found this pass, only height (10-12m per the register, up to 18m per one figure) and a description of a straight trunk with greyish-brown bark; left empty rather than guessed. SEASONAL NOTE: flowers each November (Southern Hemisphere spring), large white fragrant blooms, useful for a best_time chip later. Declared historic in 1969 and still standing and maintained by the city's Direccion General de Espacios Verdes per the 2024 Infobae piece; no dead-tree signal found. Coordinates corrected to the Wikidata item for this specific tree (Q55969455) after an initial rough street geocode was found to be ~220m off.

name: The Magnolia de Avellaneda

location.address: Av. Adolfo Berro 241, near Av. Casares, beside the Jardin Japones, Parque Tres de Febrero (Palermo Woods)

access: Free, standing in the open public parkland of Parque Tres de Febrero (Palermo Woods), open daily
transport: About 10-15 minutes' walk from Plaza Italia (Subte Line D) through the park, or several bus lines along Av. Sarmiento/Av. Figueroa Alcorta
story:
Most old trees carry an estimated age. This one carries a date. On 11 November 1875 President Nicolas Avellaneda put a magnolia into the ground with his own hands to inaugurate Parque Tres de Febrero, and the tree he planted is still standing where he left it. The arithmetic is therefore unusually honest: 151 years this November, with no growth rate and no guesswork in it.

A plaque placed in 1916 quotes the line from his inaugural speech that the choice of tree came from, la magnolia americana del bosque primitivo, con su flor blanca silvestre, the American magnolia of the primeval forest with its wild white flower. In June 1946 a national decree made it an Arbol Historico, putting it on the short list of trees the Argentine state protects for what happened around them rather than for their measurements.

Since then the park has closed in and become the Bosques de Palermo, the green lung the whole neighbourhood is named for. The Jardin Japones went up alongside, so the tree that opened the park now stands against a garden wall on Avenida Berro, passed by joggers who have no idea it is the reason any of this is here.

Come in the southern spring, when the heavy white flowers open. That is roughly the same few weeks each year as the anniversary of the day it went in.

best_time.label: October and November, when the big white flowers open, close to the anniversary of its planting

verify_notes_removed: DOCUMENTED PLANTING DATE for this specific tree, not the garden around it: planted by President Dr. Nicolas Avellaneda with his own hand at the inauguration ceremony of Parque Tres de Febrero on 11 November 1875, per the city's own Arbopedia register and Argentina.gob.ar's national-monuments page. Age is a direct calculation from that date (2026 minus 1875 = 151 years), not a growth-rate guess, so it is given as a tight band around 150 rather than the broad century-wide band a derived growth estimate would need. Declared an Arbol Historico by National Decree No. 2232 of 4 June 1946 (the same decree that covers the Pacara de Segurola, see leads). A 1916 plaque quotes Avellaneda's own inaugural speech calling it 'la magnolia americana del bosque primitivo, con su flor blanca silvestre'. Standing beside the wall of the Jardin Japones in Palermo's Bosques de Palermo, a large, fully open public park; no access concern at all. SPECIES: same Magnolia grandiflora as the Protomedicato pair (bai_002), height given as 16m by the register versus a 10-12m 'description' height on the same page, likely the difference between an old peak estimate and a standard species-description paragraph reused verbatim across all magnolia entries on the site; recorded here for the writer's awareness. GIRTH: no trunk diameter or circumference published; left empty rather than guessed. SEASONAL NOTE: flowers in spring (Southern Hemisphere, roughly October-November), which lines up with the planting anniversary in November, a nice detail for best_time. No dead-tree signal found; multiple recent press mentions (a May 2026 La Nacion feature) treat it as standing today.

name: The Esterculia of Plaza Lavalle

location.address: Plaza Lavalle, near Av. Cordoba and Talcahuano

access: Free, standing in the open public Plaza Lavalle, in front of the Teatro Colon and the Palacio de Justicia, open at all hours
transport: A few minutes' walk from Subte Line D, Tribunales station, or Subte Line B, Uruguay station
story:
Two trees of this species are known in the whole of Buenos Aires, and this is the one with an address. Sterculia coccinea is a tropical species from Southeast Asia, and the city's register lists it among the notable trees of Buenos Aires on rarity alone rather than for size or age: about eight metres tall, heavily branched, with a crown that spreads wider than the tree stands high. Its flowers come yellow green flushed with red in spring, and later in the year the capsules split open to show a bright red lining.

The address is the point as much as the tree is. Plaza Lavalle sits between the Teatro Colon and the Palacio de Justicia, so this quiet tropical outsider has spent its life between the country's opera house and its supreme court, with the crowds that both of those attract passing underneath it.

Nobody has dated it. No register, plaque or article we could find gives an age or a trunk measurement, and an empty field is better than an invented number. If you know when it went in, tell us and we will put it on the page.

The pin marks the plaza rather than the trunk, so give yourself a minute to pick it out from the trees around it: look for the wide, low, many-branched crown near the Cordoba and Talcahuano corner.
verify_notes_removed: RARITY rather than age is the story here: the city's own register (Arbopedia, listed under 'Arboles y Plantaciones Notables de la Ciudad', a step below full 'Arbol Historico' status) says this is one of only two known specimens of Sterculia coccinea in the whole city, a tropical Southeast Asian species in the Malvaceae family (formerly classified under Sterculiaceae). About 8m tall, very branched with a wide spreading crown, yellow-green flowers tinged red in spring, capsule fruits with a bright red interior in summer-autumn. NO AGE given by any source found this pass and none inferred; left honestly empty per the missing-age rule rather than guessed. NO GIRTH published either. LOCATION: only park-level precision, the register gives the plaza and the nearest corner (Av. Cordoba y Talcahuano) but not tree-level coordinates within the block-sized plaza, so marked approximate; a future pass or reader could tighten this with a photo or a walk-through. ACCESS: fully open, no concern, Plaza Lavalle is one of downtown Buenos Aires's best-known public plazas, fronting the Teatro Colon and the Palacio de Tribunales (courts). No dead-tree signal found; the city's own current register page lists it as an existing notable specimen. Worth checking in a future pass whether the second known specimen of this species in the city (unnamed, location not found this pass) is findable and worth adding.
